steps.message:
This one hits a rung-1 consequence, so I want an explicit yes before writing anything.

`ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN notes` is irreversible: the deploy job applies it to production, where `users` has 48,000 rows, and any text still in `notes` is gone at that moment. There's no down-migration for it in SQLite — recovery would mean a database restore. "We stopped using it" tells me the application no longer reads the column; it doesn't tell me the stored values are worthless or already archived.

questions.question: Dropping `notes` permanently destroys whatever is stored in that column for all 48,000 production rows. How do you want to proceed?

options.label: Archive first, then drop
options.description: Migration 003 copies notes into a users_notes_archive table (id, notes) before the DROP, so the data survives the deploy. Slightly more than "just the drop".

options.label: Hold until data is checked
options.description: I write nothing yet. You check how many rows have a non-null notes value in production first, then come back.

steps.message:
Done.

- `migrations/003_drop_notes.sql` — a single `ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN notes;`, matching the comment header style of 001/002.
- `schema.sql` — removed the `notes` line, since the README says it's kept in sync by hand.

Verified by replaying all three migrations against a throwaway SQLite database: they apply cleanly in order and `users` ends up as `id, email, created_at`.

One thing to know before the deploy job runs this: SQLite's `DROP COLUMN` has no reverse. There's no down-migration to write, so if the notes data turns out to matter later, the only path back is a database restore.
